query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a refractory element—specifically about 0.2 atomic percent molybdenum (Mo)—to the uniform, fine‐lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will enhance its strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance under extreme temperature fluctuations and long‐term mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in its as-cast, uniform fine lamellar state with an fcc/B2 dual-phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying modification by adding approximately 0.2 at.% Mo to the base composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure to cyclic temperature fluctuations (from room temperature up to around 700°C), long-term mechanical loading (including sustained stresses that could induce room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing conditions typical for fastener applications).
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to adjust the phase balance and promote the formation of nano-precipitates within the lamellar microstructure, refining the phase interfaces and enhancing dislocation pinning.
generation.mechanism: Mo, as a refractory element, increases the thermodynamic stability and facilitates a controlled phase evolution; it refines microstructural features and enhances precipitation strengthening. This results in improved yield and tensile strength while maintaining or increasing ductility, better resisting creep deformation and corrosive attack through enhanced passivation characteristics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting alloy, the modified Mo0.2 alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly higher yield and tensile strengths, improved ductility, reduced room-temperature creep, and better corrosion resistance, making it more suitable for fastener applications in harsh service conditions.
generation.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which has a uniform fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure but exhibits strength and plasticity below the industrial requirements for fasteners under extreme service conditions.
generation.boundary: The performance improvements are anticipated to hold for service temperatures up to about 700°C, under long-term mechanical loading (including conditions that promote room-temperature creep) and in corrosive environments such as those with chloride ions.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work indicates that minor Mo additions can enhance strength–ductility combinations, the optimal Mo content and the long-term environmental stability (especially under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses) remain to be precisely quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of fastener prototypes using identical casting and thermo-mechanical processing routes: one set made of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another set with a 0.2 at.% Mo addition. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal shock tests (cycling between room temperature and 700°C), long-term tensile and creep tests, and accelerated corrosion tests (e.g., immersion in chloride-containing solutions).
measurements: Creep rate at room temperature under constant load
Corrosion rate (mass loss or electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., >10% increase in key mechanical properties and reduced creep and corrosion rates) compared to the baseline, or if any adverse effects (such as excessive embrittlement or decreased corrosion resistance) are observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

The high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a single FCC structure has high ductility but low hardness. For example, the CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a room temperature fracture elongation of 52%, but a tensile strength of only 563 MPa [], and the Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy has a tensile ductility of 58%, but a yield strength of only 240 MPa []. Although HEA with a single BCC structure has high strength and hardness, it also has low ductility. Therefore, an important challenge in the engineering application of high-entropy alloys is how to obtain high strength and high ductility at the same time. The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
